title: The Ottoman Empire
subtitle: 1299–1517 · From Frontier Principality to Imperial Capital: Bursa, Edirne, Constantinople and the Conquest of the Arab Lands

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Osman to Selim I, the Çandarlı viziers and Mahmud Pasha, and the dynasty's rules of succession

entries.label: Osman I
entries.hint: Osman, the leader of a Turkmen frontier band in north-west Anatolia, gave his name to the dynasty and the people; the traditional date of 1299 for the beginning of his rule is a later convention, and the earliest source for him, a Greek chronicle, reports his victory over a Byzantine force at Bapheus near Nicomedia about 1301–1302. Nothing is known of his career from contemporary Ottoman sources, which date from over a century later.
entries.note: Pachymeres, Historia 4.25–26; Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002); Cemal Kafadar, Between Two Worlds (1995).

entries.label: Orhan
entries.hint: Orhan took Bursa after a long siege in 1326 and made it the first capital, took Nicaea in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, absorbed the neighbouring emirate of Karasi about 1345 and, through his son Süleyman, secured a fort at Çimpe on the Dardanelles in 1352 and Gallipoli in 1354, so establishing a bridgehead in Europe. His marriage with Theodora, daughter of John VI Kantakouzenos, and his service as an ally in the Byzantine civil wars gave him the entrance to the Balkans.
entries.note: John Kantakouzenos, Histories 3–4; Gregoras; Imber 2002; Kafadar 1995.

entries.label: Murad I
entries.hint: Murad took Adrianople (Edirne) about 1369 and made it the capital, defeated the Serbian lords at the Maritsa in 1371, brought the Bulgarian tsars and the Byzantine emperor into vassalage and organised the Janissary corps and the beylerbeylik of Rumelia; he was killed at Kosovo in 1389, by a Serbian noble according to most accounts. His reign laid the base of Ottoman rule in the Balkans.
entries.note: Imber 2002; Halil İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age (1973); Neşri, Cihânnümâ.

entries.label: Bayezid I Yıldırım
entries.hint: Bayezid, the Thunderbolt, annexed most of the Anatolian emirates, besieged Constantinople from 1394, destroyed a crusade at Nicopolis in 1396 and took the title Sultan of Rum, but he alienated the Turkmen princes whose lands he annexed and was beaten and captured by Timur at Ankara in 1402; he died in captivity in 1403.
entries.note: Neşri; Ibn Arabshah, Timur; Aşıkpaşazade; Imber 2002.

entries.label: The Interregnum and Mehmed I
entries.hint: After Ankara the sons of Bayezid fought each other for eleven years: Süleyman held Rumelia, Musa his brother with a Serbian and Wallachian backing, Mehmed Anatolia and İsa a part of it; Mehmed defeated Musa in 1413 and restored the state as Mehmed I, with the help of the Byzantine emperor Manuel II, and ruled until 1421. The crisis was remembered later as a reason for the practice of fratricide.
entries.note: Dukas, Historia Turco-Byzantina; Aşıkpaşazade; Dimitris Kastritsis, The Sons of Bayezid (2007).

entries.label: Murad II
entries.hint: Murad II suppressed the pretender Mustafa, besieged Constantinople in 1422 and took Thessaloniki from Venice in 1430, annexed Serbia in 1439 and, after abdicating in favour of his son Mehmed in 1444, returned to command the army at Varna and again in the second battle of Kosovo in 1448; he was a patron of a cultured court at Edirne and died in 1451, leaving the throne to Mehmed II.
entries.note: Imber, The Crusade of Varna (2006); Neşri; Dukas; İnalcık 1973.

entries.label: Mehmed II the Conqueror
entries.hint: Mehmed II, who took Constantinople at 21 in 1453, spent the rest of his reign taking Serbia (1459), the Morea (1460), Trebizond (1461), Bosnia (1463), Karaman (1468) and Euboea (1470) and the Crimean ports (1475), and failed at Belgrade in 1456 and Rhodes in 1480; he rebuilt the capital, issued the first legal codes and centralised the state, and died on campaign in May 1481.
entries.note: Kritovoulos, History of Mehmed the Conqueror; Franz Babinger, Mehmed the Conqueror and His Time (1953); İnalcık 1973; Imber 2002.

entries.label: Bayezid II
entries.hint: Bayezid II won the throne against his brother Cem in 1481 and ruled for three decades, consolidating the conquests of his father, taking Kilia and Akkerman on the Black Sea (1484), waging an inconclusive war with the Mamluks in 1485–1491 and building the first large fleet of the empire; he was pressed to abdicate in 1512 by his son Selim with the support of the Janissaries and died soon after.
entries.note: Neşri; Selahattin Tansel, Sultan II. Bayezit'in Siyasi Hayatı (1966); Imber 2002.

entries.label: Selim I Yavuz
entries.hint: Selim I came to the throne by forcing his father to abdicate, after a civil war with his brothers Ahmed and Korkud, whom he had killed; he defeated Shah Ismail at Chaldiran in 1514, took Aleppo, Damascus and Cairo from the Mamluks in 1516–1517 and became the protector of the holy cities, doubling the empire in eight years. He died in 1520 and was succeeded by Süleyman.
entries.note: İdris-i Bitlisi, Selim-nâme; Ibn Iyas, Badāʾiʿ al-zuhūr; Imber 2002; Ahmed Uğur, The Reign of Sultan Selim I (1985).

entries.label: The Çandarlı viziers
entries.hint: A family of Turkish jurists from İznik provided the chief vizier or kadi to Murad I and his successors, among them Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Elder, Halil Hayreddin and Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger, who as grand vizier advised peace with Byzantium; Mehmed II had the last Halil arrested and executed soon after the fall of Constantinople, ending the family's hold and favouring slave-origin viziers.
entries.note: Doukas; Kritovoulos; İnalcık 1973.

entries.label: Mahmud Pasha Angelović
entries.hint: Mahmud Pasha, born to a Serbian-Byzantine family and taken into the sultan's service by devshirme or capture, was grand vizier from 1456 to 1468 and again from 1472 to 1474 and led the conquests of Serbia, the Morea, Bosnia and Trebizond; he was also a patron of poetry and of architecture, built a mosque and a bath, and was executed in 1474 on a charge of treason, a sign of the slave-vizier's insecurity.
entries.note: Kritovoulos; Babinger 1953; Theoharis Stavrides, The Sultan of Vezirs (2001); İnalcık 1973.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Kosovo, Nicopolis, Ankara, Varna, the fall of Constantinople, the Venetian war, Chaldiran and the conquest of Syria and Egypt

entries.label: The battle of Kosovo
entries.hint: At Kosovo Polje on St Vitus Day Murad I's army met a Serbian coalition under Prince Lazar with Bosnian and other contingents; both Lazar and Murad were killed and the result is unclear in the sources, but Serbia became a tributary of Bayezid, and the battle took on a central place in Serbian memory as a defeat and a sacrifice, later in a national myth.
entries.note: Imber 2002; Mehmed Neşri; Serbian sources (Constantine the Philosopher); Thomas Emmert, Serbian Golgotha (1990).

entries.label: Nicopolis
entries.hint: A crusade of Hungarian, French, Burgundian and other knights under King Sigismund besieged Nikopol on the Danube and was routed by Bayezid I, who killed some of his prisoners and ransomed the nobles for heavy sums; the defeat ended the last crusade of the central Middle Ages in the Balkans.
entries.note: Froissart; Schiltberger, Reisebuch; Aziz Atiya, The Crusade of Nicopolis (1934).

entries.label: The battle of Ankara
entries.hint: Timur invaded Anatolia in response to the appeals of the dispossessed emirs and the grievances against Bayezid, and in the plain at Ankara the Tatar cavalry broke the Ottoman army, whose Anatolian troops went over to their former princes; Bayezid was captured and Timur restored the emirates, so for a decade the Ottoman state ceased to exist as a single power.
entries.note: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Ibn Arabshah; Ruy González de Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane (1403–1406).

entries.label: The battle of Varna
entries.hint: The crusade of Władysław III of Poland-Hungary and János Hunyadi broke the Peace of Szeged, which Murad II had just made, and at Varna the king was killed and the crusaders routed; the victory secured the Ottoman hold on Thrace and Bulgaria and left Constantinople without any hope of a western relief force.
entries.note: Callimachus, Historia de rebus gestis a Vladislao; Imber 2006.

entries.group: Constantinople and the Wars of Mehmed II
entries.label: The conquest of Constantinople
entries.hint: Mehmed II besieged the city for 53 days with an army of some 60,000–80,000, a fleet dragged over land into the Golden Horn and the great cannon cast by the Hungarian Orban, against a garrison of 7,000–8,000 under Constantine XI Palaiologos and Giovanni Giustiniani; the walls fell at a final assault on 29 May. The city was sacked for three days and became the capital of the Ottoman state.
entries.note: Doukas; Kritovoulos; Nicolò Barbaro, Diary of the Siege of Constantinople; Steven Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965).

entries.group: Constantinople and the Wars of Mehmed II
entries.label: The siege of Belgrade
entries.hint: Mehmed II's attempt to take Belgrade, the gateway to Hungary, was beaten back by János Hunyadi's relief force and a crusader army under John of Capistrano; the sultan was wounded and retreated, and Hunyadi died of plague a month later. Belgrade stayed Hungarian until 1521.
entries.note: Kritovoulos; John of Capistrano, letters; Imber 2002.

entries.group: Constantinople and the Wars of Mehmed II
entries.label: The Ottoman–Venetian war
entries.hint: Sixteen years of war with Venice over the Morea, Negroponte (Euboea, taken in 1470 after a long siege) and Albania, where Skanderbeg's resistance ended with his death in 1468 and the fall of Shkodër in 1479; the treaty of 1479 gave Venice peace for an indemnity of 100,000 ducats and an annual payment of 10,000 for her trading rights, with the surrender of Shkodër, Lemnos and the Mani, and made the sultan the first power in the Aegean.
entries.note: Kenneth Setton, The Papacy and the Levant vol. 2 (1978); Imber 2002.

entries.group: Constantinople and the Wars of Mehmed II
entries.label: Rhodes and Otranto
entries.hint: In 1480 a fleet under Mesih Pasha attacked Rhodes, defended by the Knights Hospitaller under Pierre d'Aubusson, and was repulsed after weeks of bombardment, and another force under Gedik Ahmed Pasha took Otranto on the Italian heel and held it until after Mehmed's death in 1481; the two events showed the limit of the sultan's naval reach.
entries.note: Guillaume Caoursin, Obsidionis Rhodiae urbis descriptio (1480); Setton 1978.

entries.label: The Ottoman–Mamluk war of 1485–1491
entries.hint: Bayezid II's armies fought the Mamluks of Qaytbay over the marches of Cilicia, Dulkadir and Karaman, with Ottoman defeats in 1485 and 1486 and Mamluk losses in 1488; the war ended in a peace that left the borderland in Mamluk hands, a rebuff that Selim redressed in 1516.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas vol. 3; Imber 2002; Petry 1994.

entries.label: Chaldiran
entries.hint: Selim I, after a campaign across eastern Anatolia and the persecution of the Qizilbash in his lands, met Shah Ismail's cavalry at Chaldiran in Azerbaijan, where the Ottoman guns and Janissary muskets broke the Safavid horse; Selim took Tabriz for a few days, but returned for want of supplies, and the war began the long Ottoman–Safavid rivalry and left eastern Anatolia and the Kurdish lords in Ottoman hands.
entries.note: İdris-i Bitlisi; Hasan-i Rumlu, Ahsanü't-tevarih; Imber 2002.

entries.label: Marj Dabiq and Ridaniya
entries.hint: At Marj Dabiq near Aleppo in August 1516 Selim's artillery destroyed the Mamluk army and killed Sultan Qansuh al-Ghawri, and after Ottoman entry into Damascus and Gaza the army defeated Tumanbay at Ridaniya outside Cairo on 22 January 1517; Tumanbay was hanged at the Zuwayla gate and the Mamluk state was ended, bringing Syria, Egypt and the Hijaz under the Ottomans.
entries.note: Ibn Iyas, Badāʾiʿ al-zuhūr vol. 5; Ibn Zunbul; Carl Petry, Protectors or Praetorians? (1994).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The devshirme and Janissaries, the timar, the kanun of Mehmed II and the communities of the capital

entries.label: The Janissaries and the devshirme
entries.hint: The kapıkulu, the sultan's slave troops, grew from a corps of prisoners and then of Christian boys taken in the Balkans, the devshirme, who were converted, trained and given as soldiers and officials; the Janissaries, the infantry core, were first raised under Murad I or Murad II and became a standing army paid in coin, an institution that over time ran in competition with the old Turkish aristocracy.
entries.note: Basilike Papoulia, Ursprung und Wesen der Knabenlese im Osmanischen Reich (1963); İnalcık, 'Ghulām', EI2; Kafadar 1995.

entries.label: The timar system
entries.hint: Cavalrymen, the sipahis, were given the revenue of a village or group of villages, a timar, and kept armed troops in proportion to its yield, with the central survey registers, the tahrir defters, recording the taxpayers and the sources of income; the system meant that the state paid its provincial army without cash and gave the sultan a record of his taxable land.
entries.note: İnalcık, 'Timar', EI2; Imber 2002; Tahrir defters (Başbakanlık Osmanlı Arşivi).

entries.label: The annexation of the Anatolian principalities
entries.hint: The Ottomans absorbed the Turkmen beyliks of Saruhan, Aydın, Menteşe, Germiyan and Karaman, often by marriage or purchase and sometimes by force, and Mehmed II completed the work in 1468–1475 with the end of the Karamanid dynasty, the largest rival state in the peninsula; the settlement of timars and the transfer of local elites to the capital followed.
entries.note: Imber 2002; Kafadar 1995; Neşri.

entries.label: The Greek patriarchate and the millet
entries.hint: After the conquest Mehmed II had a monk, George Scholarios, who had opposed union with Rome, elected as Patriarch Gennadios II in 1454 and gave him civil authority over the Orthodox subjects with the rights to manage their own law of marriage, inheritance and charity; the Armenian patriarchate at Istanbul and the chief rabbi followed, and what was later called the millet system was formed over the following centuries.
entries.note: Gennadios Scholarios, Works; Benjamin Braude and Bernard Lewis (eds.), Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Empire (1982).

entries.label: The kanunname of Mehmed II
entries.hint: Mehmed II's code, the Kanunname, set the order of the court and the officials, their salaries and their precedence, and included the clause that the sultan who comes to the throne may lawfully put his brothers to death for the good of the world order, which his successors used; its issue marked the sultan's claim to lay down law alongside the sharia.
entries.note: Kanunname-i Âl-i Osman (Mehmed II), ed. Friedrich Kraelitz (1921); İnalcık 1973; Imber, Ebu's-Su'ud (1997).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Hagia Sophia, the Greek patriarchate, Sheikh Bedreddin, the Sephardi refuge and the Qizilbash

entries.label: The Bektashi and Mevlevi orders
entries.hint: The Bektashi order, which honoured Hacı Bektaş Veli and combined Sufi and heterodox Shia elements, became the order associated with the Janissaries from the late fifteenth and sixteenth century, while the Mevlevis of Konya, following the poet Rumi, enjoyed the patronage of the court; both orders and many dervish lodges (zaviyes) formed the religious frontier of the early state.
entries.note: Irène Mélikoff, Hadji Bektach (1998); Kafadar 1995.

entries.label: Sheikh Bedreddin
entries.hint: Bedreddin, a former judge of Musa Çelebi and a teacher of Sufi and philosophical learning, led a rising in 1416 of Turkmen, peasants and Christians in the Aydın and Deliorman regions, with a teaching of common property and a shared divine presence, and was captured and hanged by Mehmed I's forces at Serres; his followers were the Bedreddinis and he became a figure in Turkish radical memory.
entries.note: Şerifî, Şeyh Bedreddin Menâkıbnâmesi; Dukas; Michel Balivet, Islam mystique et révolution armée dans les Balkans ottomans (1995).

entries.label: Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque
entries.hint: On the afternoon of the conquest Mehmed II entered Hagia Sophia, where thousands had taken refuge, and ordered that it be made the principal mosque of the city; the altar was removed, a mihrab and later minarets were added, and Hagia Sophia remained a mosque until 1934, became a museum, and was reconverted to a mosque in 2020.
entries.note: Kritovoulos 1.70; Doukas 39; Robert Mark and Ahmet Çakmak, Hagia Sophia from the Age of Justinian to the Present (1992).

entries.label: The refuge of the Sephardim
entries.hint: After the expulsion from Spain in 1492 Bayezid II is said to have admitted the Jewish refugees and to have remarked that the Spanish king had impoverished his own kingdom; tens of thousands of Sephardim settled in Istanbul, Salonica, Izmir and Safed, where they started printing presses and brought their languages and trades.
entries.note: Joseph Hacker, 'Ottoman policy toward the Jews', in Christians and Jews in the Ottoman Empire (1982); Stanford Shaw, The Jews of the Ottoman Empire (1991).

entries.label: Selim I and the Qizilbash
entries.hint: After the Şahkulu rising of 1511 in Antalya, supported by the Safavids, Selim, as the governor of Trabzon and then as sultan, had the Qizilbash of Anatolia registered and many of them killed or deported in 1514, in numbers for which a figure of 40,000 is given in later sources; the persecution deepened the break between the Sunni state and the Alevi heterodox Turkmen.
entries.note: Hasan-i Rumlu, Ahsanü't-tevarih; Imber 2002; Kafadar 1995.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The mosques of Bursa and Edirne, the Topkapı, Bellini's Mehmed and the court poets

entries.label: The Ottoman court poets
entries.hint: Ahmedi's Iskendername (c. 1390), a long Turkish epic and the first Ottoman history in verse, and the poets of Mehmed II's court, Ahmed Pasha, Necati and the sultan himself under the pen-name Avni, show the growth of a Turkish literary language in Persian forms; Necati's divan became a model for later Ottoman poets.
entries.note: E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry vol. 1–2 (1900–1902); Walter Andrews, Poetry's Voice, Society's Song (1985).

entries.label: The mosques of Bursa
entries.hint: The Ulu Cami, a large mosque with twenty domes, was built in 1396–1399 by Bayezid I as a thank-offering for Nicopolis, and the Yeşil Cami and tomb (1419–1424) of Mehmed I with tiles of blue and green are examples of the early Ottoman style; Bursa, with the tombs of the first sultans, became a sacred city of the dynasty.
entries.note: Godfrey Goodwin, A History of Ottoman Architecture (1971); Aptullah Kuran, The Mosque in Early Ottoman Architecture (1968).

entries.label: The Üç Şerefeli mosque at Edirne
entries.hint: Murad II's mosque, with its four minarets, one with three balconies (üç şerefeli), and the large central dome of 24 metres that spanned a space without interior supports, was a step toward the grand Ottoman domed mosques of Sinan and prepared the plan of the Selimiye.
entries.note: Goodwin 1971; Kuran 1968.

entries.label: Topkapı Palace
entries.hint: Mehmed II began the Topkapı, the New Palace, on the first hill above the Golden Horn in 1459 and finished the main courts, the Imperial Council, the treasury and the tiled pavilion (Çinili Köşk) by 1478; it was the residence of the sultans until the nineteenth century and its plan of successive courts expressed the order of the court.
entries.note: Gülru Necipoğlu, Architecture, Ceremonial, and Power: The Topkapı Palace (1991).

entries.label: Bellini's portrait of Mehmed II
entries.hint: At the request of the Venetian government after the peace of 1479, the Venetian painter Gentile Bellini went to Istanbul in 1479–1481 and painted the sultan in a half-length portrait, now in the National Gallery in London, set in a Renaissance arch and with a triple crown; the portrait, a rare event for a Muslim ruler, shows Mehmed's interest in Italian art, and he also collected Western medals and books.
entries.note: National Gallery, London NG3099; Julian Raby, Venice, Dürer and the Oriental Mode (1982); Babinger 1953.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Italian humanism at the sultan's court, Ali Qushji, the early chronicles and the ghazi thesis

entries.label: The ghazi thesis and its critics
entries.hint: Paul Wittek argued in 1938 that the early Ottoman state was driven by the ethos of the ghazi, the holy warrior for Islam, which explained its expansion; later historians, among them Colin Imber, Rudi Lindner and Heath Lowry, said that the Ottomans were a tribal confederacy that took Christians into their ranks and fought for plunder and power, while Cemal Kafadar proposed a frontier society in which both motives and confessions mixed.
entries.note: Paul Wittek, The Rise of the Ottoman Empire (1938); Lindner, Explorations in Ottoman Prehistory (2007); Kafadar 1995.

entries.label: The first Ottoman chronicles
entries.hint: The Ottomans' own history was written only a century after Osman, in the works of Ahmedi, Yahşi Fakih (lost, but cited by Aşıkpaşazade), Aşıkpaşazade's Tevarih-i Al-i Osman (c. 1480), Oruç Beğ and Neşri's Cihannüma, whose accounts of Osman's dreams, of Ottoman descent from the Oghuz and of the early conquests are legend as much as record.
entries.note: Aşıkpaşazade; Oruç Beğ; Neşri; Kafadar 1995; Imber 2002.

entries.label: Mehmed II and Italian humanism
entries.hint: Mehmed II kept Greek scholars such as George Amiroutzes and Kritovoulos at his court, read Ptolemy, Homer and Livy, had Amiroutzes prepare an Arabic version and a map from Ptolemy's Geography and called himself the successor of the Roman emperors; Kritovoulos' History of Mehmed the Conqueror presented him as a new Alexander, and Italian visitors and the painter Bellini reported on his interests.
entries.note: Kritovoulos, History; Babinger 1953; Necipoğlu 1991; Raby 1982.
keywords: Kritovoulos History of Mehmed the Conqueror

entries.label: Ali Qushji and the Fatih madrasas
entries.hint: The Fatih complex included eight madrasas, the Sahn-ı Seman, where the Samarkand astronomer Ali Qushji, a pupil of Ulugh Beg, taught after his move to Istanbul in 1472; Ali Qushji's work on the motion of the planets, the book on astronomy dedicated to Mehmed and a discussion of whether philosophy could be separated from natural science influenced later Ottoman thought.
entries.note: Ali Qushji, Risāla fī al-hayʾa; Sabra, 'Ali Qushji' in Dictionary of Scientific Biography; İnalcık 1973.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Bursa silk, the repopulation of the capital, the Balkan mines and the akçe

entries.label: Coinage and the akçe
entries.hint: The first Ottoman silver coin, the akçe, struck under Orhan about 1326, was debased several times in the fifteenth century, among them the recoinage of Mehmed II's reign in the 1470s; the sultan's fiscal pressure, including the confiscation of waqf and freehold lands in the mid-1470s, caused opposition among the ulema and the old aristocracy.
entries.note: Şevket Pamuk, A Monetary History of the Ottoman Empire (2000); İnalcık 1973.

entries.label: The silk of Bursa
entries.hint: Bursa was the terminal of the caravans that brought Iranian raw silk to the Mediterranean, where Genoese and Venetian merchants bought it and Italian cloth and spices were sold in return; the Ottoman state taxed the silk market and built the covered bazaar, the Koza Han, in 1491, and the city became the first great commercial centre of the dynasty.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'Bursa and the commerce of the Levant', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 3 (1960); Imber 2002.

entries.label: The resettlement of Constantinople
entries.hint: After 1453 the city, which had perhaps 30,000–50,000 inhabitants, was repopulated by forced transfers (sürgün) of Muslims, Greeks, Armenians and Jews from conquered towns in Anatolia and the Balkans and by gifts of property; by the 1470s it had grown to some 60,000–70,000 and by the 1520s to several hundred thousand.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'Istanbul', EI2; Heath Lowry, The Nature of the Early Ottoman State (2003); Kritovoulos.

entries.label: The silver of Serbia and Bosnia
entries.hint: The conquest of the Serbian despotate in 1455–1459 gave the sultan the silver and gold mines of Novo Brdo, Srebrenica and others, which supplied the mints of Edirne and Constantinople with the metal for the akçe, a silver coin; the mines were worked by Saxon and local miners under Ottoman regulations.
entries.note: Desanka Kovačević-Kojić, Gradski život u Srbiji i Bosni (1973); Halil Sahillioğlu, in An Economic and Social History of the Ottoman Empire (1994).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Rumelihisarı, Orban's cannon, the arsenal and the Janissary firearm

entries.label: The arsenal and the navy at Gallipoli
entries.hint: The Ottoman navy, begun at Gallipoli in the fourteenth century under Turkish and renegade captains, grew into a state arsenal with several tens of galleys by Mehmed II's reign, and under Bayezid II, with the help of the corsair Kemal Reis, the first major sea fights with Venice were fought in 1499–1503, including the victory at Zonchio.
entries.note: Idris Bostan, Osmanlı Bahriye Teşkilatı (1992); Imber 2002.

entries.label: The Janissary firearm
entries.hint: Hand firearms, the tüfek, were used by Janissaries by the 1440s, and became their characteristic weapon in the late fifteenth century, with the wagon fort and the cannon of the Hungarian and Hussite practice; Ottoman gunpowder weapons were decisive at Chaldiran and Marj Dabiq, and they were a main reason for the superiority over the Mamluk and Safavid cavalry.
entries.note: Ágoston 2005; Imber 2002; David Ayalon, Gunpowder and Firearms in the Mamluk Kingdom (1956).

entries.label: Rumelihisarı
entries.hint: Mehmed II built, within four and a half months, a fortress on the European shore of the Bosphorus at its narrowest point opposite the earlier Anadoluhisarı of Bayezid I, to control the straits and cut off Constantinople from the Black Sea; with three great towers and a thick wall, it was one of the preparations of the siege.
entries.note: Kritovoulos 1.10; Doukas 34; Necipoğlu 1991; Ágoston 2005.

entries.label: Orban's cannon
entries.hint: Orban, a Hungarian founder who had offered his skills first to the Byzantine emperor, cast a bronze bombard at Edirne that threw a stone ball of some 500–600 kilograms for about a mile, and others of different sizes; the guns breached the Theodosian walls in the siege, though they were slow to load and some burst, and showed the importance of siege artillery to the sultan's methods.
entries.note: Doukas 35; Kritovoulos 1.27; Barbaro; Gábor Ágoston, Guns for the Sultan (2005).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Venetian treaty, Galata, Cem Sultan, the Crimean khanate and the Aq Qoyunlu

entries.label: The Venetian treaty and the Galata capitulation
entries.hint: The Genoese colony of Galata surrendered on terms to Mehmed II on 1 June 1453, keeping its privileges, and in April 1454 Venice, which had lost its quarter, concluded a treaty giving the Venetian bailo at Istanbul his own court and Venetian merchants a fixed custom of two per cent; the privileges were the model of the later capitulations.
entries.note: Treaty of 18 April 1454 (Venice, Archivio di Stato); Halil İnalcık, 'Imtiyāzāt', EI2.

entries.label: The Aq Qoyunlu and Venice
entries.hint: Venice sought allies against Mehmed II in the east, and Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu, who ruled Iran and Iraq and had a Byzantine wife of the Trebizond house, promised an alliance and was defeated at Otluk Beli in 1473 by the Ottoman army, which had firearms the Turkmen lacked; the failure ended the plan of a general coalition.
entries.note: Setton 1978; John Woods, The Aqquyunlu (1976); Josafa Barbaro, Travels to Tana and Persia.
keywords: Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu

entries.label: The Crimean khanate
entries.hint: In 1475 Gedik Ahmed Pasha took the Genoese port of Caffa and the Crimean coastal towns, and the khan Mengli Giray, who had been supported by the sultan against his rival, became a vassal; the arrangement gave the sultan a Tatar ally with a large cavalry against Poland, Muscovy and Hungary until 1774.
entries.note: Alan Fisher, The Crimean Tatars (1978); İnalcık, 'Mehmed II', EI2.

entries.label: Cem Sultan
entries.hint: Cem (Jem), the son of Mehmed II who lost the war of succession to Bayezid II in 1481, fled to the Mamluks and then to the Knights of Rhodes, who sent him to France and then to the pope; Bayezid paid the Knights and the pope an annual sum for keeping him captive, and the prince was a weapon in the plans for a crusade until his death at Naples in 1495.
entries.note: Nicolas Vatin, Sultan Djem (1997); Setton 1978.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The plague, the settlement of Rumelia and the new capital

entries.label: Seljuk and Turkmen migrations after Mongol rule
entries.hint: The Mongol victory at Köse Dağ in 1243 and the fall of the Seljuks of Rum drove Turkmen nomads to the western marches, where they formed the emirates, and the Ottoman state was one of these; its early rise was owed in part to a location near the Byzantine borderlands, where the plunder of frontier warfare was greatest.
entries.note: Claude Cahen, The Formation of Turkey (2001); Kafadar 1995; Vryonis 1971.

entries.label: Plague in the Ottoman lands
entries.hint: Plague arrived with the Black Death in 1347–1348 and returned every decade or so, and in the Balkan campaigns of Murad II and Mehmed II armies and cities were hit, as at Constantinople in the 1440s and at Belgrade in 1456; the population of Anatolia and the Balkans stood below its earlier level through much of the fifteenth century.
entries.note: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977); Nükhet Varlık, Plague and Empire in the Early Modern Mediterranean World (2015).

entries.label: Turkish settlement in Rumelia
entries.hint: After Gallipoli, nomad groups and colonists from Anatolia were settled in Thrace and Macedonia, with places named Yürük and the lands near Edirne, Serres and Skopje filled with Muslim villages and with religious foundations; the registers of 1455–1520 show the proportions of Muslims and Christians in each district.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'Ottoman methods of conquest', Studia Islamica 2 (1954); Speros Vryonis, The Decline of Medieval Hellenism (1971); Lowry 2003.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The devshirme boys, the sipahi, the sultan's mothers and wives, and the captives

entries.label: The sultans' mothers and wives
entries.hint: Ottoman sultans married Byzantine, Serbian and Turkmen princesses in the early period as political acts: Theodora with Orhan, Mara Branković with Murad II, who after his death was sent home and was a diplomat in her own right, and the daughters of the emirs; from the mid-fifteenth century they took concubines who bore the heirs, and the mother of a prince governed his province with him.
entries.note: Leslie Peirce, The Imperial Harem (1993); Dukas; Kafadar 1995.

entries.label: The captives and the slave trade
entries.loc: The Black Sea and the Balkans
entries.hint: Raids across the Danube and into Hungary, Wallachia and Albania, and by the Crimean Tatars into Poland and Russia, brought tens of thousands of captives to Ottoman markets at Edirne, Gallipoli and Istanbul, where a fifth of the captives was by law the sultan's due, the pençik; slaves worked in households, on estates and in the army.
entries.note: Halil İnalcık, 'Servile labor in the Ottoman Empire', in The Mutual Effects of the Islamic and Judeo-Christian Worlds (1979); Imber 2002.

entries.label: The devshirme boys
entries.hint: Every few years officials took one boy in forty households, usually between eight and twenty, from Christian villages in the Balkans, registered them and sent them to Turkish farms or to Istanbul for training; the best became pages, Janissaries or governors. Their families' accounts, as in Serbian and Greek laments, speak of grief, and the Ottoman sources of the pashas who rose in this way show a mixed picture.
entries.note: Papoulia 1963; Ottoman devshirme registers (Başbakanlık Osmanlı Arşivi); Metin Kunt, The Sultan's Servants (1983).

entries.label: The sipahi and the peasant
entries.hint: The tahrir registers show a rural society of Christian and Muslim households taxed in kind and in cash, with a sipahi's timar yielding perhaps 3,000 to 20,000 akçe a year, and the peasant owing him dues and labour; the taxes on peasants were generally lower than in the late Byzantine or Serbian states, which some historians have seen as a reason for local acceptance of Ottoman rule.
entries.note: Tahrir defters; İnalcık, 'Ottoman methods of conquest' (1954); Lowry 2003.
